Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).

B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

{"content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, along with 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 425,431 with criminal convictions of some kind. The agency knows who these people are and is not holding them.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 involved non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The number of noncitizens sentenced federally has fallen 27% since fiscal 2018, so the federal backstop is handling a smaller share of the caseload even as the docket ICE cannot detain has grown.
- Jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 ICE detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for the non-detained docket, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements, and require DHS to publish these numbers on a schedule.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had entered the country illegally in 2022. A Georgia judge sentenced him in November 2024 to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Nothing in the handling of his immigration case made his removal anyone's priority until a young woman was dead.

That is the cost of an interior enforcement system that tracks people rather than taking them into custody. Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is not a rhetorical flourish. It is ICE's own accounting of its non-detained docket, provided to Congress in September 2024 in response to a letter from Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas. As of July 21, 2024, that docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions, and 425,431 convicted criminals overall.

Precision matters here, because this figure is often flattened in the retelling. Non-detained means ICE is not holding them; it does not mean no one is. DHS has said the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under administrations of both parties, and ICE has never disclosed how many people on the list are currently serving sentences in federal, state or local custody. What is not in dispute is the agency's own description of the docket: cases it is tracking, not cases it is resolving. Some of those 13,099 will finish a prison term this year, next year or a decade from now and walk out of a state facility with no detainer honored and no ICE bed funded to receive them.

The docket is not an argument that every illegal alien is dangerous; most are not. It is an argument that the federal government has already identified the population that most needs to be detained and removed, has told Congress exactly how large it is, and has not been given the resources or the legal authority to act on it.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal criminal system tells the same story from a different angle. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentencing cases in fiscal 2024, of which 21,304 involved non-U.S. citizens. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences fell on noncitizens. Among those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

These are the cases federal prosecutors chose to bring. GAO found that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to 21,500. A shrinking federal caseload is not evidence of a shrinking problem. It means the system meant to backstop state justice is carrying a smaller share of the criminal-alien caseload than it carried five years ago, at the same moment ICE reports hundreds of thousands of convicted criminals on a docket it lacks the beds to hold.

The federal numbers also mark the limit of federal responsibility. A federal sentence ends in federal custody and a supervised release. An immigration case that ends nowhere, as most non-detained docket cases do, ends with the alien back in the community. The gap between those two outcomes is where public safety is lost.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that records the immigration status of everyone it convicts, which makes Department of Public Safety data the best state-level evidence available and, for that reason, the most contested. Two research organizations that have worked through the same records reach opposite conclusions.

The Cato Institute, analyzing DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000 residents, against 3.0 for native-born Americans and 1.2 for legal immigrants. On that reading, illegal immigrants are about 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than the native-born, and Cato flags real quality problems in the non-homicide data. The Center for Immigration Studies argues that Cato's denominators miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison, and concludes that the same data show illegal immigrants convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average.

Both readings cannot be right, and the disagreement itself is a finding: the United States does not collect crime data by immigration status well enough to settle the question, and anyone selling certainty either way is ahead of the evidence. What no reading disputes is the numerator. Every year of that period, Texas convicted illegal immigrants of homicide, and each conviction is a person killed by someone who should not have been in the country and could have been removed. Even the more favorable estimate yields 2.2 preventable homicides per 100,000 residents. That is an argument for enforcement, not against it, and it is reason for Congress to require the data that would end the argument.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

An ICE detainer marks the point where a state sentence ends and federal immigration enforcement is supposed to begin. It asks a jail to hold a deportable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so ICE can take custody. Where the request is honored, the removal happens. Where it is declined, the door opens and the alien is gone.

ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happens at that door. Between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025, jails and prisons in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, more than half of them in California, and in more than 1,400 instances failed to give ICE adequate notice of a pending release so no officer was present at all. Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000. In 72 cases the alien released despite a detainer had a homicide conviction or charge.

Seventy-two is not a rounding error in a national debate. It is 72 people who had already killed, or been charged with killing, released by a policy choice rather than transferred to federal custody. Every one of those cases passed through a jail that knew ICE wanted the person and let him go anyway.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention beds, transport and removal capacity sized to the criminal caseload ICE has already identified, and direct the Secretary of Homeland Security to prioritize for arrest and removal every noncitizen on the docket with a homicide, sexual assault or weapons conviction. A docket of 13,099 homicide convictions is a work queue, not a report.
2. **Condition federal funds on detainer compliance.** Withhold specified federal law enforcement and criminal justice grants from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers or fail to notify ICE of a pending release, and give state and local agencies clear statutory authority to honor detainers.
3. **Expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements.** Fund the jail model of the 287(g) program so partner agencies screen inmates and transfer deportable convicts directly to ICE, prioritizing jurisdictions whose own policies currently bar cooperation.
4. **Require regular public reporting.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly and without waiting for a congressional letter, the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the number of detainers declined by jurisdiction, and every release of an alien with a homicide or sexual assault conviction. A number this consequential should not depend on who asks.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, along with 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 425,431 with criminal convictions of some kind. The agency knows who these people are and is not holding them.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 involved non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The number of noncitizens sentenced federally has fallen 27% since fiscal 2018, so the federal backstop is handling a smaller share of the caseload even as the docket ICE cannot detain has grown.
- Jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 ICE detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for the non-detained docket, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements, and require DHS to publish these numbers on a schedule.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had been paroled into the country after entering illegally near El Paso in September 2022. He was arrested in New York the following year on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could lodge a detainer, and he then failed to report his move to Georgia as his release required. A Georgia judge sentenced him in November 2024 to life in prison without the possibility of parole. In the eighteen months between his arrival and her death, immigration enforcement never had hold of him.

That is the cost of an interior enforcement system that tracks people rather than taking them into custody. Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is not a rhetorical flourish. It is ICE's own accounting of its non-detained docket, provided to Congress in September 2024 in response to a letter from Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas. As of July 21, 2024, that docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions, and 425,431 convicted criminals overall.

Precision matters here, because this figure is often flattened in the retelling. Non-detained means ICE is not holding them; it does not mean no one is. DHS has said the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under administrations of both parties, and ICE has never disclosed how many people on the list are currently serving sentences in federal, state or local custody. What is not in dispute is the agency's own description of the docket: cases it is tracking, not cases it is resolving. Some of those 13,099 will finish a prison term this year, next year or a decade from now and walk out of a state facility with no detainer honored and no ICE bed funded to receive them.

The docket is not an argument that every illegal alien is dangerous; most are not. It is an argument that the federal government has already identified the population that most needs to be detained and removed, has told Congress exactly how large it is, and has not been given the resources or the legal authority to act on it.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal criminal system tells the same story from a different angle. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentencing cases in fiscal 2024, of which 21,304 involved non-U.S. citizens. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences fell on noncitizens. Among those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

These are the cases federal prosecutors chose to bring. GAO found that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to 21,500. A shrinking federal caseload is not evidence of a shrinking problem. It means the system meant to backstop state justice is carrying a smaller share of the criminal-alien caseload than it carried five years ago, at the same moment ICE reports hundreds of thousands of convicted criminals on a docket it lacks the beds to hold.

The federal numbers also mark the limit of federal responsibility. A federal sentence ends in federal custody and a supervised release. An immigration case that ends nowhere, as most non-detained docket cases do, ends with the alien back in the community. The gap between those two outcomes is where public safety is lost.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes Department of Public Safety data the best state-level evidence available and, for that reason, the most contested. Two research organizations that have worked through the same records reach opposite conclusions.

The Cato Institute, analyzing DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000 residents, against 3.0 for native-born Americans and 1.2 for legal immigrants. On that reading, illegal immigrants are about 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than the native-born, and Cato flags real quality problems in the non-homicide data. The Center for Immigration Studies argues that Cato's denominators miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison, and concludes that the same data show illegal immigrants convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average.

Both readings cannot be right, and the disagreement itself is a finding: the United States does not collect crime data by immigration status well enough to settle the question, and anyone selling certainty either way is ahead of the evidence. What no reading disputes is the numerator. Every year of that period, Texas convicted illegal immigrants of homicide, and each conviction is a person killed by someone who should not have been in the country and could have been removed. Even the more favorable estimate yields 2.2 preventable homicides per 100,000 residents. That is an argument for enforcement, not against it, and it is reason for Congress to require the data that would end the argument.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

An ICE detainer marks the point where a state sentence ends and federal immigration enforcement is supposed to begin. It asks a jail to hold a deportable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so ICE can take custody. Where the request is honored, the removal happens. Where it is declined, the door opens and the alien is gone.

ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happens at that door. Between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025, jails and prisons in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, more than half of them in California, and in more than 1,400 instances failed to give ICE adequate notice of a pending release so no officer was present at all. Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000. In 72 cases the alien released despite a detainer had a homicide conviction or charge.

Seventy-two is not a rounding error in a national debate. It is 72 people who had already killed, or been charged with killing, released by a policy choice rather than transferred to federal custody. Every one of those cases passed through a jail that knew ICE wanted the person and let him go anyway.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention beds, transport and removal capacity sized to the criminal caseload ICE has already identified, and direct the Secretary of Homeland Security to prioritize for arrest and removal every noncitizen on the docket with a homicide, sexual assault or weapons conviction. A docket of 13,099 homicide convictions is a work queue, not a report.
2. **Condition federal funds on detainer compliance.** Withhold specified federal law enforcement and criminal justice grants from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers or fail to notify ICE of a pending release, and give state and local agencies clear statutory authority to honor detainers.
3. **Expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements.** Fund the jail model of the 287(g) program so partner agencies screen inmates and transfer deportable convicts directly to ICE, prioritizing jurisdictions whose own policies currently bar cooperation.
4. **Require regular public reporting.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly and without waiting for a congressional letter, the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the number of detainers declined by jurisdiction, and every release of an alien with a homicide or sexual assault conviction. A number this consequential should not depend on who asks.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*

It assembles federal and state data on illegal aliens convicted of serious crimes who are not in immigration custody.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, along with 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 425,431 with criminal convictions of some kind. The agency knows who these people are and is not holding them.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 involved non-U.S. citizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The number of noncitizens sentenced federally fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, so the federal backstop is handling a smaller share of the caseload even as the docket ICE cannot detain has grown.
- Jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 ICE detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for the non-detained docket, condition federal funds on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements, and require DHS to publish these numbers on a schedule.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had been paroled into the country after entering illegally near El Paso in September 2022. He was arrested in New York the following year on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could lodge a detainer, and he then failed to report his move to Georgia as his release required. A Georgia judge sentenced him in November 2024 to life in prison without the possibility of parole. In the 18 months between his arrival and her death, immigration enforcement never had hold of him.

That is the cost of an interior enforcement system that tracks people rather than taking them into custody. Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is not a rhetorical flourish. It is ICE's own accounting of its non-detained docket, provided to Congress in September 2024 in response to a letter from Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas. As of July 21, 2024, that docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions, and 425,431 convicted criminals overall.

Precision matters here, because this figure is often flattened in the retelling. Non-detained means ICE is not holding them; it does not mean no one is. DHS has said the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under administrations of both parties, and ICE has never disclosed how many people on the list are currently serving sentences in federal, state or local custody. What is not in dispute is the agency's own description of the docket: cases it is tracking, not cases it is resolving. Some of those 13,099 will finish a prison term this year, next year or a decade from now and walk out of a state facility with no detainer honored and no ICE bed funded to receive them.

The docket is not an argument that every illegal alien is dangerous; most are not. It is an argument that the federal government has already identified the population that most needs to be detained and removed, has told Congress exactly how large it is, and has not been given the resources or the legal authority to act on it.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal criminal system tells the same story from a different angle. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentencing cases in fiscal 2024, of which 21,304 involved non-U.S. citizens. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences involved non-U.S. citizens. Among those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

These are the cases federal prosecutors chose to bring. GAO found that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to 21,500. A shrinking federal caseload is not evidence of a shrinking problem. It means the system meant to backstop state justice is carrying a smaller share of the criminal-alien caseload than it carried five years ago, at the same moment ICE reports hundreds of thousands of convicted criminals on a docket it lacks the beds to hold.

The federal numbers also mark a limit. A criminal sentence ends in custody, then supervised release. A case that sits on the non-detained docket ends wherever the person happens to be living, which is to say in an American community. The distance between those two outcomes is where public safety is lost.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes Department of Public Safety data the best state-level evidence available and, for that reason, the most contested. Two research organizations that have worked through the same records reach opposite conclusions.

The Cato Institute, analyzing DPS conviction records for 2013 through 2022, puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal aliens at 2.2 per 100,000 residents, against 3.0 for native-born Americans and 1.2 for legal aliens. On that reading, illegal aliens are about 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than the native-born, and Cato flags real quality problems in the non-homicide data. The Center for Immigration Studies argues that Cato's denominators miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison, and concludes that the same data show illegal aliens convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average.

Both readings cannot be right, and the disagreement itself is a finding: the United States does not collect crime data by immigration status well enough to settle the question, and anyone selling certainty either way is ahead of the evidence. What no reading disputes is the numerator. Every year of that period, Texas convicted illegal aliens of homicide, and each conviction is a person killed by someone who should not have been in the country and could have been removed. Even the more favorable estimate yields 2.2 preventable homicides per 100,000 residents. That is an argument for enforcement, not against it, and it is reason for Congress to require the data that would end the argument.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

An ICE detainer marks the point where a state sentence ends and federal immigration enforcement is supposed to begin. It asks a jail to hold a deportable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so ICE can take custody. Where the request is honored, the removal happens. Where it is declined, the door opens and the alien is gone.

ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happens at that door. Between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025, jails and prisons in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, more than half of them in California, and in more than 1,400 instances failed to give ICE adequate notice of a pending release so no officer was present at all. Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000. In 72 of those cases, the alien released despite a detainer had a homicide conviction or charge.

Seventy-two is not a rounding error in a national debate. It is 72 people who had already killed, or been charged with killing, released by a policy choice rather than transferred to federal custody. Every one of those cases passed through a jail that knew ICE wanted the person and let him go anyway.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention beds, transport and removal capacity sized to the criminal caseload ICE has already identified, and direct the Secretary of Homeland Security to prioritize for arrest and removal every noncitizen on the docket with a homicide, sexual assault or weapons conviction. A docket of 13,099 homicide convictions is a work queue, not a report.
2. **Condition federal funds on detainer compliance.** Withhold specified federal law enforcement and criminal justice grants from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers or fail to notify ICE of a pending release, and give state and local agencies clear statutory authority to honor detainers.
3. **Expand 287(g) jail enforcement agreements.** Fund the jail model of the 287(g) program so partner agencies screen inmates and transfer deportable convicts directly to ICE, prioritizing jurisdictions whose own policies currently bar cooperation.
4. **Require regular public reporting.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly and without waiting for a congressional letter, the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the number of detainers declined by jurisdiction, and every release of an alien with a homicide or sexual assault conviction. A number this consequential should not depend on who asks.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute.*
